claims.text: The nature of element X governs whether CrFeCoNiX retains a stable protective oxide above 900 °C.
Al-containing CrFeCoNiX forms an oxide whose crystal structure closely matches the metallic matrix.
Si-containing CrFeCoNiX forms an oxide whose crystal structure closely matches the metallic matrix.
Oxides formed by Al- or Si-containing CrFeCoNiX have thermal expansion closely matching that of the metallic matrix.
Crystallographic and thermal-expansion matching relieves interfacial or growth-induced stresses.
Reduced interfacial stress causes the oxide scale to remain adherent and minimizes spallation.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX forms a less coherent oxide that is prone to cracking or spallation.
Element X reacts with oxygen and contributes to formation and evolution of the surface oxide.
Mn-derived oxide lacks the structural and thermal-expansion compatibility attributed to Al- or Si-derived oxides.
The Mn-containing oxide scale becomes unstable under thermal cycling.
Al- or Si-containing CrFeCoNiX will form a slow-growing oxide layer.
Al- or Si-containing CrFeCoNiX will form a continuous, coherent oxide layer that persists at high temperature.
CrFeCoNiMn will develop a less adherent scale that cracks or spalls under the same exposure conditions.
CrFeCoNiMn lacks a strongly reactive element that forms a structurally compatible protective oxide.
The proposed comparison uses CrFeCoNiAl, CrFeCoNiSi, and CrFeCoNiMn samples in similar solid-solution states under identical oxidative exposure.
The hypothesis is restricted to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
Small compositional changes and phase distributions may alter oxide matching and oxidation kinetics.
